AnimatedContainer.explanation: AnimatedContainer is a stateful widget that smoothly changes supported Container properties when its values change. It uses the given duration and curve, while its child and descendants remain unchanged by this animation.

interview.question: What does AnimatedContainer do?
interview.answer: It is an implicit animation widget based on Container. When supported property values change, it animates from the old values to the new values using duration and curve.
interview.followUp: How would you build a more complex animation? Use an AnimatedWidget subclass such as DecoratedBoxTransition, or manage an AnimationController yourself.

interview.question: What are duration and curve used for?
interview.answer: The duration is required and controls how long the parameter transition takes. The curve controls the timing pattern used during that transition.
interview.followUp: What happens if duration is omitted? The constructor call is invalid because duration is a required parameter.

interview.question: Which values can it animate?
interview.answer: The widget can animate values such as alignment, padding, color, decoration, size constraints, margin, and transform. A null value is not animated.
interview.followUp: Are the widget's children animated too? No. The child and its descendants are outside AnimatedContainer's implicit property animation.

keyPoints: It provides an animated version of Container.
When supported property values change, it transitions from the old value to the new value.
The curve sets the timing style, and duration sets the transition length.
It can hold a child like a normal Container.
onEnd can run after each animation finishes.
clipBehavior controls clipping when a decoration exists.
gotchas: A null property does not take part in the animation.
Changing the child does not animate the child or its descendants.
Use either color or decoration. Color is shorthand for a colored BoxDecoration.

interview.question: What is the role of AnimationController?
interview.answer: It owns the changing animation value and provides controls such as forward, reverse, stop, and setting value. It also implements Animation<double>, so widgets that accept an Animation can use it.
interview.followUp: How do you animate another type? Chain a Tween or another Animatable to the controller, often with drive.

interview.question: Why is vsync required?
interview.answer: The controller needs a TickerProvider through vsync. A State commonly supplies it by using SingleTickerProviderStateMixin.
interview.followUp: What changes if a state needs several controllers? Use a ticker provider suitable for multiple tickers, such as the corresponding ticker-provider mixin.

interview.question: How do bounds and duration affect the controller?
interview.answer: The default bounded controller moves from lowerBound to upperBound, which default to 0.0 and 1.0, over duration. reverseDuration can specify a different duration when moving backward.
interview.followUp: When would you use unbounded? Use AnimationController.unbounded when the value should not be limited by upperBound or lowerBound.

interview.question: Where is AppBar normally used, and what can it contain?
interview.answer: AppBar is normally assigned to Scaffold.appBar. It displays the toolbar, including leading, title, and actions, and can also display bottom and flexibleSpace widgets.
interview.followUp: How would you make an app bar scroll? Use SliverAppBar inside a CustomScrollView instead of placing a normal AppBar in Scaffold.appBar.

interview.question: How does AppBar choose a leading widget?
interview.answer: When leading is null and automatic inference is enabled, Flutter adds a drawer button if the Scaffold has a Drawer. Otherwise, it adds a BackButton when the Navigator has a previous route.
interview.followUp: How do you prevent this automatic leading widget? Set automaticallyImplyLeading to false.

interview.question: How is AppBar height determined?
interview.answer: The preferred height is based on toolbarHeight plus the height of bottom. If toolbarHeight is null, preferredHeightFor can use the toolbar height from AppBarTheme.
interview.followUp: What is commonly placed in bottom? A TabBar is the usual choice for tabs arranged across multiple pages.

flexibleSpace is drawn behind the toolbar and bottom, and its height matches the full AppBar height.

build.sourceTitle: build method - Builder class - widgets library - Dart API
build.summary: The build method describes a widget's user interface subtree. Flutter calls it when the widget is inserted or an inherited dependency changes, and it must return widgets without side effects.
build.explanation: A widget's build method describes the user interface below that widget. Flutter calls it when the widget enters the tree and when an inherited dependency changes. It should create and return widgets without side effects. Its result may update the current subtree or replace it, depending on whether the existing root can be updated.

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: The location in the widget tree where this widget is being built. It also provides access to inherited widgets for that location.

build.returns: A Widget that represents the subtree below this widget.

example.title: A simple build method
example.explanation: The framework calls this method to create the widget subtree for the current context.

useCases.scenario: Read inherited values available at the current tree location.

useCases.scenario: Choose or configure child widgets using the current BuildContext.

interview.question: When does Flutter call build?
interview.answer: Flutter calls build when the widget is inserted into the tree and when one of its inherited dependencies changes. The method returns the widget subtree for that location.
interview.followUp: What should build avoid? It should avoid side effects because Flutter may call it in every frame.

interview.question: What are BuildContext and the return value used for?
interview.answer: Build receives a BuildContext and returns a Widget. The context identifies the widget's location and gives access to inherited widgets for that location.
interview.followUp: Can the same widget receive different contexts? Yes. This can happen when it moves in the tree or is inserted in multiple places.

interview.question: How does Flutter handle the widget returned by build?
interview.answer: The returned widget becomes the subtree below the current widget. Flutter updates the existing subtree or creates a new one based on whether Widget.canUpdate can update its root.
interview.followUp: What should be used when build needs other changing state? Use a StatefulWidget when that dependency is not a stable field or inherited value.

keyPoints: build describes the portion of the user interface represented by the widget.
Flutter calls build when the widget is inserted into the tree.
Flutter can call build again when an inherited dependency changes.
The returned widget defines the subtree below the current widget.
A build implementation usually creates and returns a new group of configured widgets.
gotchas: Do not perform side effects in build. Flutter may call it during any frame.
A StatelessWidget build method should use stable widget fields and inherited values from context.
Use StatefulWidget when building depends on changing data that is not available through the widget fields or inherited context.

interview.question: What is BuildContext?
interview.answer: BuildContext is a handle for a widget's location in the widget tree. Flutter passes it to build methods and makes it available through State.context.
interview.followUp: Why can two contexts in one build method behave differently? A context belongs to a particular element, so inherited lookups begin at that element's location.

interview.question: How does BuildContext affect inherited widgets?
interview.answer: Inherited lookups start from the context's location and search its ancestors. Therefore, Theme.of(context) finds the nearest Theme above that context.
interview.followUp: How can code access a widget created inside the same build method? Use a Builder to obtain a context for that subtree.

interview.question: What does BuildContext.mounted mean?
interview.answer: The mounted property says whether the associated widget is still in the tree. Context operations are valid only while mounted is true, and an unmounted context does not become mounted again.
interview.followUp: What should asynchronous callbacks do? Check context.mounted after the await and before navigation or another context operation.

keyPoints: BuildContext represents a widget's location in the widget tree.
APIs such as Theme.of and showDialog use a context to act for a widget or find related data.
Use Builder when you need a context belonging to a subtree created inside build.
BuildContext is an interface over an Element, which discourages direct element manipulation.
A context's location may change when its widget moves in the tree.
gotchas: Do not cache values obtained from a BuildContext after the current synchronous function ends.
The context passed to build belongs to the current widget, not to widgets returned by build.
After awaiting an asynchronous operation, check mounted before using the context.

interview.question: What is ChangeNotifier used for?
interview.answer: ChangeNotifier is a class that can be extended or mixed in. It provides a change-notification API based on VoidCallback and implements Listenable.
interview.followUp: How can a model use it with widgets? A model can become a Listenable and work with widgets such as ListenableBuilder, allowing listening widgets to rebuild when the model changes.

interview.question: How does notification work?
interview.answer: Call addListener to register a callback. When the model changes, call notifyListeners to invoke the registered callbacks.
interview.followUp: What should a model method do after changing its data? It should update the data first, then call notifyListeners so clients observe the new state.

interview.question: What are the performance costs?
interview.answer: Adding a listener is O(1). Removing listeners and dispatching notifications are O(N), where N is the number of listeners.
interview.followUp: Which operation becomes more costly as listeners increase? Removing listeners and sending notifications, because both are linear in the listener count.

interview.answer: Column arranges children vertically. Its width is the greatest child width, and mainAxisSize controls whether its height uses the maximum available height or shrinks to the children.

interview.question: When should Expanded be used?

interview.question: How should a vertically growing layout be handled?

interview.question: What is Container used for?
interview.answer: Container is a convenience widget that combines common painting, positioning, and sizing widgets. It can manage padding, margin, alignment, constraints, decoration, and transforms.
interview.followUp: When would a simpler widget be better? Use Padding, Align, SizedBox, or DecoratedBox when only one focused behavior is needed.

interview.question: How does Container choose its size?
interview.answer: With a child and no overriding size settings, Container passes the parent constraints to the child and usually sizes itself to match the child. Width, height, constraints, and alignment can change this behavior.
interview.followUp: What happens without a child? Under bounded constraints it expands to the available constraints; under unbounded constraints it tries to be as small as possible.

interview.question: What is Container's painting order?

Null safety.explanation: Dart's `Null` class represents the single object denoted by `null`. It is a special class that does not implement `Object`, and Dart provides operators to test, replace, assign, call through, or spread values that may be null.

interview.question: What is the Dart `Null` class?
interview.answer: `Null` is the type of the single object represented by the reserved word `null`. It is the only class that does not implement `Object`.
interview.followUp: Can a class extend `Null`? No. Attempting to extend or implement it is a compile-time error.

interview.question: What are `??` and `??=` used for?
interview.answer: `??` returns its left operand unless that operand is null; otherwise, it returns the right operand. `??=` assigns the right operand only when the variable is null.
interview.followUp: How can you call a method only when a value exists? Use `?.`, such as `value?.foo()`.

interview.question: What happens when Dart uses the `!` operator on null?
interview.answer: `!` asserts that an expression is not null and throws if that assumption is false. The nullable spread form `...?` includes the value's elements only when the value is not null.
interview.followUp: What does `?.` do? It calls the member only if the receiver is not null; otherwise, the call is skipped.

gotchas: The non-null assertion operator `!` throws when the value is null.

setState.sourceTitle: setState method - State class - widgets library - Dart API
setState.summary: setState tells Flutter that a State object's internal value changed. Flutter then schedules that State object to build again so its subtree can reflect the change.
setState.explanation: Call setState when a State object's internal value changes and that change can alter its user interface. Put only the synchronous state change inside the callback; do asynchronous work before or after it.

useCases.title: Separate state updates from side effects

interview.question: What does setState do?
interview.answer: setState runs the callback immediately and synchronously. It then marks the element as needing a build, so Flutter can rebuild the State object.
interview.followUp: What happens if the value changes without setState? Flutter might not schedule a build, so the displayed subtree might not reflect the new value.

interview.question: Why can the setState callback not be async?
interview.answer: The callback must not be async and must not return a Future. Perform the asynchronous operation outside the callback, then put the synchronous state update in setState.
interview.followUp: Why should file or network work stay outside the callback? The callback tells Flutter exactly when the state change occurs; asynchronous work would make that timing unclear.

interview.question: How should setState be used for performance?
interview.answer: setState has little direct overhead, but it can cause a widget subtree to rebuild and may trigger layout and painting. Call it only when the resulting build output changes meaningfully.
interview.followUp: Is calling setState twice useful in one frame? No. The documentation says repeated calls provide no benefit for the same State during that frame.

keyPoints: Use setState to tell Flutter that internal state changed.
After the callback, Flutter schedules this State object for a build.
Keep unrelated calculations and side effects outside the callback.
A direct change without setState might leave the user interface unchanged.
Its core behavior is to run the callback synchronously and mark the element for rebuilding.
gotchas: Do not make the callback async or return a Future. Finish asynchronous work outside setState, then update state synchronously.
Do not call setState after dispose. Cancel timers, animation listeners, and other callbacks that could run after removal.

interview.question: What does SizedBox do?
interview.answer: SizedBox is a widget for requesting a specific width and height. With a child, it tries to make the child fit those dimensions while following the parent’s constraints.
interview.followUp: What happens when width or height is null? With a child, SizedBox uses the child’s size in that dimension; without a child, the missing dimension is treated as zero.

interview.question: What is SizedBox.expand used for?
interview.answer: SizedBox.expand makes the box as large as its parent allows. It is equivalent to using double.infinity for both width and height.
interview.followUp: How can you make a fixed-size child work inside a tight parent? Put it under a widget such as Center or Align that permits a smaller size.

interview.question: Why might a SizedBox be ignored?

interview.followUp: How does SizedBox differ from ConstrainedBox? SizedBox exposes explicit width and height, while ConstrainedBox accepts arbitrary BoxConstraints.

interview.answer: Stack places children on top of one another. Non-positioned children determine the stack's size and use alignment; Positioned children use top, right, bottom, and left values.

interview.question: Describe the State lifecycle.
interview.answer: The framework creates State with StatefulWidget.createState. It associates the State with a BuildContext, calls initState and didChangeDependencies, and then may call build repeatedly.

interview.question: How should internal state changes be reported?

interview.question: Describe the State lifecycle.
interview.answer: The framework creates State, associates it with a permanent BuildContext, then calls initState, didChangeDependencies, build, and later dispose. After dispose, the object is unmounted and cannot be mounted again.
interview.followUp: When is didChangeDependencies useful? Use it for initialization involving inherited widgets, especially when depending on an inherited widget can change.

interview.followUp: What happens if the stream emits faster than Flutter builds? The builder receives a timing-dependent ordered subset of snapshots, including the final one.

Streams.explanation: A Stream delivers asynchronous data events, error events, and one final done event. You can read it with await for or register callbacks with listen. A stream normally allows one listener or many listeners, depending on whether it is single-subscription or broadcast.

interview.question: What is a Stream?
interview.answer: A stream is a source of asynchronous events. Events can contain data or errors, and one done event marks the end. You can consume it with await for or listen.
interview.followUp: How can one source support several listeners? Convert a single-subscription stream with asBroadcastStream, then add multiple listeners.

interview.question: How do single-subscription and broadcast streams differ?
interview.answer: A single-subscription stream accepts only one listener over its lifetime and starts producing events when listened to. A broadcast stream supports multiple listeners and emits events whether listeners are present or not.
interview.followUp: Which type commonly fits file input? A single-subscription stream, because it represents chunks from one continuous data source.

interview.question: What does listen return and why is it useful?
interview.answer: listen registers callbacks and returns a StreamSubscription. The subscription can stop listening or pause event delivery. Other stream methods are built on this lower-level operation.
interview.followUp: How can stream data be changed? Use transformations such as where, skip, expand, or asyncMap, which return another stream.

keyPoints: A stream delivers events over time instead of returning all values at once.
Events are either data values or error notifications.
A single done event signals that no more events will arrive.
Use await for inside an async or async* function to read stream data.
Use listen when callback-based control is more suitable than await for.
Broadcast streams can be shared by multiple listeners.
gotchas: Do not attach a second listener to a single-subscription stream. Canceling the first listener does not make another subscription valid.
A listener added during a broadcast event can miss that event.
Cancel a subscription when it should no longer receive events.

interview.question: What does the Text widget do?
interview.answer: Text displays a string with one style. Its style can inherit from the nearest DefaultTextStyle, and the widget can wrap or truncate text within its layout constraints.
interview.followUp: How would you display several styles in one paragraph? Use Text.rich with TextSpan children, or use RichText when more control is needed.

interview.question: How do maxLines and overflow work together?
interview.answer: maxLines limits how many lines the text may occupy. If the content needs more lines, the overflow setting controls how the extra content is shown.
interview.followUp: Is maxLines: 1 the same as softWrap: false? No. The documentation shows that fade can appear in different directions for these two cases.

interview.question: What is textScaler used for?
interview.answer: The textScaler controls font scaling during layout and rendering. If it is omitted, Text uses the ambient MediaQuery text scaler; textScaleFactor is deprecated.
interview.followUp: Why should an app avoid forcing a fixed scale? User accessibility settings normally provide the ambient scaling value, so replacing it can reduce accessible text sizing.

An inheriting TextStyle adds or overrides values while keeping inherited defaults.

textScaler defines how font size is adjusted during layout and painting.

interview.question: What is the difference between onChanged and onSubmitted?

interview.question: What is ThemeData used for?
interview.answer: ThemeData is the configuration object for a Material theme. MaterialApp can apply it to the whole app, and Theme can apply or replace it for a subtree.
interview.followUp: How does a widget read the active theme? It calls Theme.of with a BuildContext, which finds the nearest ancestor Theme.

interview.question: How are colors and text configured?
interview.answer: The constructor can use a supplied ColorScheme, or generate one from colorSchemeSeed and brightness. It also accepts a TextTheme, and components use these values to calculate defaults.
interview.followUp: What happens when both colorSchemeSeed and colorScheme are supplied? The constructor asserts that they are not both provided.

interview.question: How do you customize one component type?
interview.answer: Use component-specific properties such as sliderTheme or floatingActionButtonTheme when only one class of component needs different styling. The rest of the theme remains unchanged.
interview.followUp: How can a custom theme value be added? Define a ThemeExtension subclass, pass it in extensions, and retrieve it with extension.

keyPoints: ThemeData can define appearance for the whole MaterialApp or only one widget subtree.
Widgets use Theme.of(context) to read the active ThemeData.
Material components can rely on colorScheme and textTheme being available.
colorScheme contains the main Material color roles used by components.
You can pass a complete ColorScheme or ask ThemeData to generate one from a seed color.
Properties such as sliderTheme and bottomNavigationBarTheme customize particular component families.

interview.question: What is a Flutter Widget?
interview.answer: A Widget is an immutable description of part of the user interface. Flutter inflates it into an Element, and the Element manages the underlying render tree.
interview.followUp: What represents mutable state? Use StatefulWidget. It creates a State object when inflated and added to the tree.

interview.question: Can one Widget instance appear more than once?
interview.answer: A widget can occur multiple times in the tree. Each occurrence is inflated into a separate Element, even when the same widget object is reused.
interview.followUp: What controls replacement? The runtimeType and key are compared when Flutter updates an existing Element.

interview.question: How should mutable state be modeled?
interview.answer: Widget fields must be final because widgets are immutable configurations. For changing data tied to a widget, use StatefulWidget and its State object.
interview.followUp: When does State get created? StatefulWidget.createState creates it whenever the widget is inflated into an Element and incorporated into the tree.

keyPoints: A Widget is the configuration used to create or update an Element.
The Widget class is the base of Flutter's main UI-building class hierarchy.
Flutter turns a Widget into an Element; the Element manages the render tree below it.
Use StatefulWidget when the UI needs mutable state associated with it.
The key helps Flutter decide how a new widget replaces an old one.
Matching runtime type and key lets Flutter update the existing Element with the new widget.
gotchas: Do not store changing values in a Widget. Its fields must be final; use StatefulWidget when the widget needs mutable state.
The same widget object can be used in multiple places. Flutter inflates it separately for each placement.
